clinicalPearls: A microcephalic primordial dwarfism with severe proportionate pre- and postnatal growth restriction and marked microcephaly
The characteristic facies is often described as bird-headed, with a receding forehead, prominent beaked nose, micrognathia, and low-set dysmorphic ears
Intellectual disability is usual and typically moderate to severe, reflecting the profoundly small brain
Genetically heterogeneous, caused by biallelic variants in genes of the DNA damage response and centrosome/replication machinery, most classically ATR, with several other loci implicated
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, so consanguinity increases risk and recurrence risk to siblings is significant
Haematological complications, including cytopenias and a reported risk of myelodysplasia or leukaemia, can occur and warrant monitoring
It overlaps with other microcephalic primordial dwarfisms such as MOPD, so precise molecular diagnosis guides prognosis and counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Seckel syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous microcephalic primordial dwarfism arising from biallelic variants in genes controlling the DNA damage response, DNA replication, and centrosome function, of which ATR is the prototype. Impaired handling of replication stress and defective cell-cycle control reduce the number of cell divisions during development, most conspicuously in the brain, producing severe proportionate growth restriction and profound microcephaly. The same genome-maintenance defects underlie the associated haematological and other systemic complications.
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or exome sequencing covering ATR and other primordial dwarfism/DNA repair genes
Chromosomal microarray to exclude copy-number causes
Serial head circumference and growth measurement to characterise proportionate restriction
Full blood count monitoring for cytopenias and haematological malignancy risk
Brain imaging to assess microcephaly and any structural anomaly
redFlags: Unexplained cytopenias or features suggesting myelodysplasia or leukaemia
Signs of an intracranial vascular anomaly, which have been reported in some primordial dwarfisms
Feeding failure and severe faltering growth requiring nutritional support
reference.prognosis: Growth restriction and microcephaly are lifelong and stature remains far below normal, while cognitive impairment is usually significant. Prognosis is influenced by the specific gene involved and by haematological and other systemic complications, and survival into adulthood is possible with supportive care.
pitfalls: Grouping all microcephalic primordial dwarfisms together without molecular confirmation, obscuring differing risks
Attributing the phenotype to intrauterine environmental factors and missing the recessive genetic cause
Failing to counsel consanguineous families about substantial recurrence risk

management: Provide supportive, multidisciplinary care as there is no disease-specific or curative therapy
Offer developmental, educational and physiotherapy or occupational support for intellectual disability
Ensure nutritional support and monitor growth, recognising growth hormone is generally ineffective in this primordial dwarfism
Undertake haematological surveillance with regular full blood counts for cytopenias, myelodysplasia and leukaemia
Manage systemic and structural complications as they arise, involving relevant specialists
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, addressing consanguinity and sibling recurrence risk
Provide family screening and reproductive counselling
